sections.title: Coded Directions
sections.content: At this level, directions are given in symbols. Example: P @ Q means P is 5 meters North of Q, and P # Q means P is 8 meters East of Q. For long code equations, first write down the actual meaning of each symbol. Then determine the final position by drawing a step-by-step diagram.  Finally, find the direction or shortest distance between two points using the Pythagorean theorem.

sections.title: Multi-person Routing
sections.content: Two or three people start walking from different locations. The direction and distance of each person must be tracked separately. Create separate diagrams or a table to solve this. Finally, determine their relative positions, such as who is to the North-East of whom.

sections.title: Condition-Based Movements
sections.content: In some questions, turns are based on specific conditions. For example, turning right on even minutes and left on odd minutes. In such questions, list the time or step number and change the direction at each step. Recognizing the pattern is important.

sections.title: Use of Coordinate Geometry
sections.content: Assume an invisible grid and take the starting point as the origin (0,0).  North = +y, South = -y, East = +x, West = -x. Write the new coordinate after each move. Distance between the final two points = sqrt((x2-x1)^2 + (y2-y1)^2). This will help you find the Shortest Distance quickly.

sections.title: Complex Angles and Mixed Turns
sections.content: Understand angles like 90°, 135°, and 225° in the context of a 360° circle. If the total rotation is 450°, subtract 360° and consider it as a 90° turn. Calculating the net rotation is crucial.

sections.title: 4-6 Step Solution Strategy
sections.content: Step 1: Clarify the meaning of the code or condition. Step 2: Determine the starting point. Step 3: Convert each move into coordinates or a diagram. Step 4: Write down the final positions of all persons. Step 5: Calculate the required distance or direction. Step 6: Match with the given options.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content: 1. Interpreting the meaning of the code backward (e.g., confusing P @ Q with Q @ P). 2. Mixing up the movements of different people. 3. Adding the total distance instead of calculating the net direction/displacement. 4. Making sign errors with coordinates.

sections.title: Quick Summary
sections.content: Level 3 is a mix of coded directions, multi-person tracking, condition-based turns, and coordinate geometry. Complex questions become simpler by using systematic tables and the grid/coordinate method.

tricks.title: Decode the Code First
tricks.explanation: Write down the meaning of all symbols right at the beginning.

tricks.title: Net Coordinate Trick
tricks.explanation: Add/subtract East-West on the x-axis and North-South on the y-axis.

tricks.title: Create a Multi-person Table
tricks.explanation: Keep separate columns for each person.

tricks.title: Identify Even-Odd Patterns
tricks.explanation: Write down the pattern of direction changes for even and odd steps.
tricks.example: 1st min left, 2nd min right, 3rd min left.

tricks.title: Calculate Net Rotation
tricks.example: 270° clockwise total = same as 90° anti-clockwise (West if starting North).

tricks.title: Fast Use of Pythagoras
tricks.explanation: Remember triplets like 3-4-5, 5-12-13 and their multiples.
tricks.example: Legs of 6 and 8 = Hypotenuse of 10 (which is 2 x the 3-4-5 triplet).

tricks.title: Relative Position Shortcut
tricks.explanation: If both x and y are positive, the direction is North-East relative to the origin.

tricks.title: Final Facing Check
tricks.explanation: Always double-check the facing direction after the final turn.
tricks.example: A net 180° rotation = facing the exact opposite direction.

tricks.title: Break Down Complex Equations
tricks.explanation: Solve long coded strings in small parts.
tricks.example: In 'P @ Q # R', first map P relative to Q, then map Q relative to R.
